title: Dow Hits New Record — Then Drops on Yield Scare
text:

https://www.barrons.com/articles/dow-hits-new-record-then-drops-on-yield-scare-1538786357 Dow Hits New Record — Then Drops on Yield Scare By Oct. 5, 2018 8:39 p.m. ET Order Reprints Steve Snodgrass Text size
Is anyone else feeling déjà vu? Because last week felt a lot like February to us.
It wasn’t just that the Dow Jones Industrial Average reached an all-time high before getting hit. The blue-chip benchmark dropped 11.26 points, to 26,447.05, while the S&P 500 fell 1%, to 2885.57. It was even worse for the Nasdaq Composite—home to tech heavyweights like Apple (ticker: AAPL), Amazon.com (AMZN), and Alphabet (GOOGL)—which tumbled 3.2%, to 7788.45.
The drop was triggered by a sudden jump in the 10-year Treasury yield, which spiked from 3.055% to 3.227% last week, its highest level since May 2011. That 0.171 percentage-point increase was the largest since—wait for it—the week ended Feb. 2. What was surprising this time was that it wasn’t the usual economic data like payrolls that caused bond yields to jump, but less-significant reports like ADP employment and the ISM services index. More in Trader Transocean’s storm-tossed stock can ride gains in oil, stronger economy
That suggests investors—who hadn’t been buying the Federal Reserve’s assessment of a strong economy and potential inflation risks—suddenly changed their minds, says Smith Capital Investors founder Gibson Smith. “Anytime there’s low volatility and high complacency, a small wake-up call can cause a move like this week’s,” he explains.
If that sounds familiar, it should. Remember, it was the sudden rise in the 10-year yield to a four-year high of 2.858% that helped spur the market’s correction earlier this year. And like then, it was the speed of the move—the 10-year yield rose 0.3 percentage point during the past month, compared with a three-year monthly average of 0.03 percentage point—that caught the market by surprise.
“The speed of changes in bond yields often matters more for equities than the level,” writes Goldman Sachs strategist Ryan Hammond.
And that sudden move left investors confused about what to do—play defense or play the rise in rates. They settled for both. The S&P 500 Financials Index rose 1.5% last week, a reasonable response given that not only was the 10-year yield rising, the yield curve was steepening with it. The latter, if sustained, would help banks, who borrow short and lend long. The S&P 500 Utilities Index, however, gained 1.9% last week, not what you’d expect from bond proxies, which usually fall when yields rise. Newsletter Sign-up
Utilities’ gains make sense given the sudden declines in the overall market, says Christopher Harvey, head of equity and quant strategy at Wells Fargo Securities. “During the equity slide, investors’ increased appetite for risk-aversion assets appeared to cause many to gravitate to the utility group,” he explains. “This is why these two groups, with very different interest rate sensitivities, both outperformed.”
Do the echoes of February—when the S&P 500 dropped 8.6% during the month’s first eight days—mean it’s time to head for the exits? Not yet, Harvey says. But with the Fed raising rates and unwinding its balance sheet, volatility should continue. And that means investors should favor high-quality companies and ones that are buying back shares.
“Investors should be taking risk out of their portfolios,” he says. “But it’s not time to run for cash and canned goods.”
